metadata.document_title: Emergency Stroke Clinical Protocol: FAST Recognition, Acute Ischemic Thrombolysis, and Urgent Triage

sections.text: A stroke is a medical emergency caused by the disruption of blood supply to part of the brain. Approximately 85% of strokes are ischemic (caused by an arterial thromboembolism or occlusion), while 15% are hemorrhagic (caused by rupture of a weakened cerebral blood vessel). Rapid community and clinical recognition relies on the FAST mnemonic: 1. Face: Facial weakness or asymmetry; one side of the face droops, and the patient may be unable to smile evenly; 2. Arms: Arm weakness or numbness; the patient cannot raise both arms or hold them outstretched; 3. Speech: Speech difficulty, slurred speech, garbled words, or total inability to speak (aphasia/dysphasia); 4. Time: Time to call emergency medical services immediately (999/911/108), noting the exact 'last known well' time, as time lost equates to irreversible cerebral neuron necrosis.

Immediate emergency department management requires urgent non-contrast head CT or brain MRI within 20-45 minutes of arrival to differentiate ischemic stroke from acute intracranial hemorrhage, as thrombolysis in hemorrhagic stroke is fatal. Capillary blood glucose must be tested immediately to exclude severe hypoglycemia (which closely mimics focal acute neurological deficits). Intravenous access, continuous cardiac monitoring, and vital sign assessment are established simultaneously.

sections.section_title: Reperfusion Time Windows: Intravenous Thrombolysis and Thrombectomy
sections.text: For acute ischemic stroke, specific evidence-based therapeutic time windows govern acute reperfusion: 1. Intravenous Thrombolysis (IV Alteplase / Tenecteplase): Administered within 4.5 hours from symptom onset ('last known well' time). Blood pressure must be controlled to < 185/110 mmHg prior to initiation; 2. Mechanical Endovascular Thrombectomy: Indicated for confirmed large vessel occlusions (LVO) of the anterior circulation (e.g., internal carotid artery or proximal middle cerebral artery M1 segment). Thrombectomy should be initiated within 6 hours of symptom onset, or up to 24 hours in selected patients demonstrating viable penumbral brain tissue on CT perfusion or diffusion-weighted MRI.
